sections.heading: Who pays a West Bloomfield rider’s medical bills

c.v: If a car or truck was involved, you have no-fault benefits, but not from your motorcycle insurer.
Under MCL 500.3114(5), your Personal Injury Protection benefits come, in order, from:

items.v: the insurer of the owner or registrant of the motor vehicle involved
the insurer of that vehicle’s operator
the motor vehicle insurer of the motorcycle’s operator
the motor vehicle insurer of the motorcycle’s owner or registrant

c.v: Priority follows the vehicles’ insurers, not who was at fault. “Involved” does not require contact; a car that cut you off is involved even if it never touched you. If no insurer in that chain exists, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan pays (MCL 500.3172), with its $250,000 medical cap, unless you owned the motorcycle and it was uninsured (MCL 500.3113(b)).
The benefits are the ones a driver would get under MCL 500.3107:

items.v: medical expenses, up to the PIP limit on the policy that pays
85 percent of lost wages for up to three years, up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each year
$20 a day in replacement services
attendant care
mileage

c.v: Written notice is due within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). See our

The first medical limit is set by a policy you did not choose. Since the 2019 reform, the PIP medical level on the policy first in priority pays first; if the driver who hit you chose $250,000, that policy pays up to $250,000, and a lower-priority policy with more coverage, such as your own car policy, may then pay the rest. This is why optional first-party medical coverage on a motorcycle policy matters.
If no car or truck was involved, no-fault does not apply.
Several common West Bloomfield crashes produce no PIP claim:

items.v: a deer strike with no other vehicle involved

a pothole or broken pavement seam on a county road

c.v: Your bills go to your health insurance and to any medical coverage you bought on the motorcycle policy. Any injury claim is against whoever caused the hazard, if anyone did.

c.v: Riders under 21 must wear a helmet. If you met those conditions, riding without a helmet was legal, so it was not a traffic violation. In a head-injury case, the insurer will argue a helmet would have reduced the injury. That is a damages and causation argument for the jury, not a bar to the claim. In a leg or shoulder case, it is irrelevant.

faqs.question: A car turned into a driveway on a lake road right in front of me. Do I have a claim?

answer.v: Usually. A driver turning left must yield to oncoming traffic, including a motorcycle. Insurers will argue your speed on the curve or hill, so photographs of the sight line and any home cameras matter. The car is “involved” under no-fault, so its owner’s insurer is first in line for your medical bills.

faqs.question: I hit a deer on my motorcycle in West Bloomfield. Who pays my medical bills?

answer.v: If no car or truck was involved, no-fault does not pay. Your health insurance and any medical coverage on your motorcycle policy pay instead, and comprehensive coverage usually pays for the bike. If a car was involved, for example one that braked or swerved and forced you down, that car’s insurer may be first in line.

faqs.question: I went down on gravel on a curve. Is anyone responsible?

answer.v: Possibly. A contractor or landscaping company that left gravel or debris on the road can be. The Road Commission can be, if it knew or should have known of a defect in the road and did not fix it in a reasonable time, with written notice within 120 days. There is no no-fault claim if no other vehicle was involved. Photograph the gravel before it is swept.

faqs.question: Does the at-fault driver’s insurance pay my medical bills?

answer.v: Not because the driver was at fault. Under the rider priority rule, the insurer of the car involved pays first, whoever caused the crash. Fault matters for your separate claim for pain and suffering.

faqs.question: I have my own car insurance. Doesn’t that cover me on the motorcycle?

answer.v: Not first. If a car was involved, that car’s insurer is first in line. Your own car insurer is third, after the involved vehicle’s owner’s and operator’s insurers. A motorcycle policy itself does not carry Michigan PIP. If no car was involved, there is usually no PIP claim at all.

faqs.question: A pothole on a West Bloomfield road caused my crash. Do I sue the township?

answer.v: No. The township does not own its public roads. The Road Commission for Oakland County does, and written notice must reach it within 120 days. A private lake-association road belongs to the association.

faqs.question: I wasn’t wearing a helmet. Can I still recover?

answer.v: Yes, if three conditions were met: - you were 21 or older - you carried the required $20,000 in medical coverage - you had either two years of endorsement or a safety course. The insurer can argue a helmet would have reduced a head injury. That goes to damages, not to whether you have a claim.

- One year to notify the responsible no-fault insurer. - Three years to sue the at-fault driver. - 120 days for a notice to the Road Commission. - 120 days for a road-defect notice against MDOT. - 120 days for a dram shop notice, and two years to sue a bar.
